parts:
Hello,

I have tried to run the Stagnant Problem in BUGS Example Vol 2 with rstan and there are errors. First, I think that there is an error in the stan syntax (file stagnant.stan.0) line 13 says vector(N) punif. I think this should be vector[N] punif. I have corrected this in my syntax below but the model fails to run. It appears the problem involves declaring int<lower=0> k; in the parameter block. I would appreciate any assistance on how to fix this issue.
Below is the rstan code I used to run the model with the vector[N] punif correction:
###This is an example file for Stan
N <- 29
x <-
  c(-1.39, -1.39, -1.08, -1.08, -0.94, -0.8, -0.63, -0.63, -0.25,
    -0.25, -0.12, -0.12, 0.01, 0.11, 0.11, 0.11, 0.25, 0.25, 0.34,
    0.34, 0.44, 0.59, 0.7, 0.7, 0.85, 0.85, 0.99, 0.99, 1.19)
Y <-
  c(1.12, 1.12, 0.99, 1.03, 0.92, 0.9, 0.81, 0.83, 0.65, 0.67,
    0.6, 0.59, 0.51, 0.44, 0.43, 0.43, 0.33, 0.3, 0.25, 0.24, 0.13,
    -0.01, -0.13, -0.14, -0.3, -0.33, -0.46, -0.43, -0.65)
###Create list for data set
dat <- list(N=N, x=x, Y=Y)

###Here is the model file
# Stagnant: a changepoint problem and an illustration of how NOT to do MCMC!
#
# Change point model with very poor parameterization stated in WINBUGS examples
stanSyn <- "
# Stagnant: a changepoint problem and an illustration of how NOT to do MCMC!
#
# Change point model with very poor parameterization stated in WINBUGS examples

data {
int<lower=0> N;
real x[N];
real Y[N];

}

transformed data {
vector[N] punif;
for (n in 1:N) punif[n] <- (1.0 / N);
}

parameters {
real alpha;
real beta[2];
int<lower=0> k;
real<lower=0> tau;
}

transformed parameters {
real sigma;
sigma <- 1 / sqrt(tau);
}

model {
tau ~ gamma(.001, .001);
alpha ~ normal(0, 1000);
for (i in 1:2) beta[i] ~ normal(0, 1000);
for (i in 1:N)
Y[i] ~ normal(alpha + beta[1 + int_step(i - k - .5)] * (x[i] - x[k]), sigma);
}
"
###This code runs stan
fit <- stan(model_code = stanSyn, model_name = "Example", data = dat, iter = 2000, chains = 3, sample_file = "stagnant.csv")

The real issue is that Stan doesn't support integer parameters.  
One approach is to take the poor parameterization of BUGS and 
marginalize out the integer parameter k.  Because k is a top 
level parameter, this requires summing out at the very top level
of the model.  The manual has more info on how to do this in the
mixture model chapter -- you need to use log_sum_exp.

They also have a continuous version of the model:

  http://www.mrc-bsu.cam.ac.uk/bugs/winbugs/Vol2.pdf

I'll try both versions and report back.  It'd be nice
to complete our collection of BUGS models :-)

- Bob

Here's a model that marginalizes out the discrete mixture-component identifier
of the BUGS "stagnant" model.

First, the BUGS model for comparison, which I took along with their output
from:

http://www.mrc-bsu.cam.ac.uk/bugs/winbugs/Vol2.pdf

model {
for (i in 1:N) {

Y[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i],tau)
    mu[i] <- alpha + beta[J[i]] * (x[i] - x[k]) 
    J[i] <- 1 + step(i - k - 0.5)
    punif[i] <- 1/N
  }
  tau ~ dgamma(0.001,0.001) 
  alpha ~ dnorm(0.0,1.0E-6) 
  for (j in 1:2)
    beta[j] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.0E-6)
  k ~ dcat(punif[])

sigma <- 1 / sqrt(tau) 
}

And here's the Stan version that marginalizes out k with a mixture
parameter theta:

// Bradley P. Carlin; Alan E. Gelfand; Adrian F. M. Smith.
// Hierarchical Bayesian Analysis of Changepoint Problems
// Applied Statistics, Vol. 41, No. 2. (1992), pp. 389-405.
//
// In these data, X represents the logarithm of the flow rate of
// water down an inclined channel (grams per centimetre per second) 
// and Y represents the logarithm of the height of the stagnant
// surface layer (centimetres) for different surfactants.

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  real x[N];
  real Y[N];
}

parameters {
  real<lower=0> sigma;
  real<lower=0> alpha;
  real beta[2];
  simplex[N] theta;
}
model {
  // local variables
  real log_probs[N];
  real mu[N];

  // priors
  theta ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(0.01,N));
  alpha  ~ normal(0,5);
  beta ~ normal(0,5);

  // mixture likelihood
  for (k in 1:N) {
for (n in 1:N)

mu[n] <- alpha + if_else(n <= k, beta[1], beta[2]) * (x[n] - x[k]);
    log_probs[k] <- log(theta[k]) + normal_log(Y, mu, sigma);
  }
  lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(log_probs);
}

Things to note:

1.  I reparameterized from precision to std deviation.  

2.  I tightened the priors on the coefficients from sd=1000 to sd=5.

3.  I marginalized out the mixture component indicator k from the original
model and gave it a Dirichlet distribution.  The model is actually very
sensitive to the Dirichlet(gamma) prior.  

4.  The posterior is very sensitive to the Dirichlet prior on the mixture.
With the Dirichlet prior set to a symmetric 0.01 prior count, the answers
are roughly the same as BUGS (including similar modes at alpha=0.5 and change
point k=15 or and alpha=1 and changepoint k = 8.  Values for the other parameters
are similar to what was reported in the BUGS volume 2 description.

Here's the print from RStan for a single chain with prior = 0.01 as in the
model above, where you can see the sampling's
still not great.  Convergence is very fast (20 or 30 iterations), but mixing remains
slow after convergence.  You can see the change point estimated to be in the 14-16
range with 75% posterior probability, which matches the traceplot in BUGS in the
mode of alpha = 0.5.

parameter theta:

// Bradley P. Carlin; Alan E. Gelfand; Adrian F. M. Smith.
// Hierarchical Bayesian Analysis of Changepoint Problems
// Applied Statistics, Vol. 41, No. 2. (1992), pp. 389-405.
//
// In these data, X represents the logarithm of the flow rate of
// water down an inclined channel (grams per centimetre per second) 
// and Y represents the logarithm of the height of the stagnant
// surface layer (centimetres) for different surfactants.

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  real x[N];
  real Y[N];
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0> sigma;
  real<lower=0> alpha;
  real beta[2];
  simplex[N] theta;
}
model {
  // local variables
  real log_probs[N];
  real mu[N];

  // priors
  theta ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(0.01,N));
  alpha  ~ normal(0,5);
  beta ~ normal(0,5);

  // mixture likelihood
  for (k in 1:N) {
    for (n in 1:N)
      mu[n] <- alpha + if_else(n <= k, beta[1], beta[2]) * (x[n] - x[k]);
    log_probs[k] <- log(theta[k]) + normal_log(Y, mu, sigma);
  }
  lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(log_probs);
}

2.  I tightened the priors on the coefficients from sd=1000 to sd=5.

model and gave it a Dirichlet distribution.  The model is actually very
sensitive to the Dirichlet(gamma) prior.  

4.  The posterior is very sensitive to the Dirichlet prior on the mixture.

model {

    J[i] <- 1 + step(i - k - 0.5)
    punif[i] <- 1/N

  alpha ~ dnorm(0.0,1.0E-6) 
  for (j in 1:2)
    beta[j] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.0E-6)
  k ~ dcat(punif[])
  sigma <- 1 / sqrt(tau)

And here's the Stan version that marginalizes out k with a mixture
parameter theta:

// Bradley P. Carlin; Alan E. Gelfand; Adrian F. M. Smith.
// Hierarchical Bayesian Analysis of Changepoint Problems
// Applied Statistics, Vol. 41, No. 2. (1992), pp. 389-405.
//
// In these data, X represents the logarithm of the flow rate of
// water down an inclined channel (grams per centimetre per second) 
// and Y represents the logarithm of the height of the stagnant
// surface layer (centimetres) for different surfactants.

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  real x[N];
  real Y[N];
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0> sigma;
  real<lower=0> alpha;
  real beta[2];
  simplex[N] theta;
}
model {
  // local variables
  real log_probs[N];
  real mu[N];

  // priors
  theta ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(0.01,N));
  alpha  ~ normal(0,5);
  beta ~ normal(0,5);

  // mixture likelihood
  for (k in 1:N) {
    for (n in 1:N)
      mu[n] <- alpha + if_else(n <= k, beta[1], beta[2]) * (x[n] - x[k]);
    log_probs[k] <- log(theta[k]) + normal_log(Y, mu, sigma);
  }
  lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(log_probs);

Here's the continuous version, which fits exactly the same
values to 2 decimal places as BUGS for posterior mean
and deviation, and converges with 4 chains.

data {
int<lower=0> N;
real x[N];
real Y[N];
}
parameters {
real<lower=0> sigma;
real<lower=0> alpha;
real beta[2];

real<lower=min(x),upper=max(x)> x_change;
}
model {
real mu[N];

alpha ~ normal(0,5);
beta ~ normal(0,5);
sigma ~ cauchy(0,5);

for (n in 1:N)
mu[n] <- alpha

+ if_else(x[n] < x_change, beta[1], beta[2]) * (x[n] - x_change);
Y ~ normal(mu,sigma);
}

I have tried to develop an extension to Bob's continuous version of the Stagnant model, for a simple case of an intercept and one covariate (data are 17 countries observed over ~50 years, N=854). It runs fine and converges quickly but I'm not confident that it's doing what I expect it to do. Here is the STAN code:

data {
    int<lower=0> N;
    real time[N];                    // time variable
    real<lower=0> lincr[N];     // y variable
    real sud[N];                     // x variable 
}
parameters {

real <lower=0> alpha;         
    real beta[2];

real gamma[2];                  
    real <lower=0> sigma;
    real<lower=5, upper=45> cp;      // change point

}
model {
    real mu[N];
    alpha ~ normal(0,5);
    beta ~ normal(0,5);

gamma ~ normal(0,5);
    sigma ~ cauchy(0,5);
for (i in 1:N)
mu[i] <- alpha +

if_else(time[i]<cp, beta[1] + gamma[1] * sud[i],
          beta[2] + gamma[2] * sud[i]) * (time[i] - cp);
    lincr ~ normal(mu, sigma);
}

My understanding is that alpha is the adjusted mean of Y, the betas are estimated differences in the mean before/after the change point, and gammas are before/after estimates of the effects of sud (a standardized measure). This could be wildly wrong since I don't really get the original Stagnant example.

I want to extend this further into a multilevel model (random intercepts with country-level predictors), and would welcome any feedback and suggestions about the model so far (syntax and interpretation).

It's a mixture. Like the one described in the manual chapter

> of the Stagnant model, for a simple case of an intercept and one covariate (data are 17 countries observed over ~50 years, N=854). It runs fine and converges quickly but I'm not confident that it's doing what I expect it to do. Here is the STAN code:
>
> data {
> int<lower=0> N;
> real time[N]; // time variable
> real<lower=0> lincr[N]; // y variable
> real sud[N]; // x variable
> }
> parameters {
> real <lower=0> alpha;
> real beta[2];
> real gamma[2];
> real <lower=0> sigma;
> real<lower=5, upper=45> cp; // change point
> }
> model {
> real mu[N];
> alpha ~ normal(0,5);
> beta ~ normal(0,5);
> gamma ~ normal(0,5);
> sigma ~ cauchy(0,5);
> for (i in 1:N)
> mu[i] <- alpha +
> if_else(time[i]<cp, beta[1] + gamma[1] * sud[i],
> beta[2] + gamma[2] * sud[i]) * (time[i] - cp);
> lincr ~ normal(mu, sigma);
> }
>

This isn't going to work well for sampling because you're
conditioning on a parameter and creating a discontinuous
desnity. It might work, but it won't be able to leverage gradients
for efficient MCMC.

Did you simulate the data and know this is recovering the right value?

Of course, values of cp between time[i] points have no meaning here --- there's
nothing to control them other than th eprior.

> My understanding is that alpha is the adjusted mean of Y, the betas are estimated differences in the mean before/after the change point, and gammas are before/after estimates of the effects of sud (a standardized measure). This could be wildly wrong since I don't really get the original Stagnant example.

Check out the manual chapter on latent discrete parameters. I
work through a simple example there.

> I want to extend this further into a multilevel model (random intercepts with country-level predictors), and would welcome any feedback and suggestions about the model so far (syntax and interpretation).

I'd try to keep the model continuously differentiable for the best
sampling, but I don't know how to do that with a continuous change point.
